title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Louisiana | Genstone
metaDescription: Louisiana investor renovations in New Orleans, Baton Rouge and Shreveport: releveling, flood history, Formosan termites, insurance-ready roofs and draws.
intro: Louisiana renovation work comes with its own vocabulary: releveling, camelbacks, raised basements, HDLC, substantial improvement, Formosan swarm season. The state's housing ranges from nineteenth-century cypress shotguns in New Orleans to mid-century brick ranches in Baton Rouge and Shreveport, and the risks shift with it, from soft soils and historic review in the south to expansive clay and ice storms in the north. Insurance has become one of the biggest variables in every deal. Genstone Construction renovates houses for fix-and-flip, BRRRR, rental, small multifamily, FHA 203(k) and REO clients in Louisiana by coordinating vetted, licensed local contractors, with a designated field manager on every project. The free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices repairs, flood exposure and insurance-sensitive items against your ARV before you commit. Each job gets a line-item scope, a draw schedule, permits handled with the right parish or city, remote documentation and no upfront payment. Our city pages cover New Orleans, Baton Rouge and Shreveport in depth.

sections.body:
New Orleans holds one of the largest collections of historic wood houses in the country. Creole cottages, shotgun singles and doubles, camelbacks and center-hall cottages fill the older riverfront neighborhoods, most built of old-growth cypress and heart pine on brick piers. Further from the river, raised basement houses and bungalows line Gentilly, Broadmoor and Mid-City, and slab ranch houses dominate New Orleans East and many suburban areas in Jefferson and St. Bernard parishes. Soft soils mean settlement and releveling are routine.

Baton Rouge has older cores in Spanish Town, Beauregard Town, the Garden District and Mid City, surrounded by large areas of 1950s through 1970s brick ranches on slabs. The August 2016 flood reached many of those neighborhoods and nearby suburbs, so flood history is a key question for any purchase there.

Shreveport's older neighborhoods, such as Highland and South Highlands, are full of early twentieth-century bungalows and revival-style homes on piers, while Broadmoor, Southern Hills and similar areas carry mid-century ranches. Expansive clay soils make foundation movement common across northwest Louisiana.

Cities such as Lafayette, Lake Charles and Monroe have their own mixes of mid-century and newer housing, and Lake Charles was heavily damaged by the 2020 hurricanes. Statewide, Formosan and native termites, humidity, pre-1978 lead paint and aging wiring and plumbing shape renovation scopes.

In New Orleans, doubles drive much of the rental market, and investors choose between keeping them as two units, converting them to singles for resale or living on one side and renting the other. Flips in historic neighborhoods succeed when they preserve character and fix structure and systems properly. Short-term rental rules are tight in most residential areas, so long-term rental income is the safer underwriting assumption.

Baton Rouge offers BRRRR and buy-and-hold opportunities in mid-century ranch neighborhoods, student and staff rentals near LSU and Southern University, and flips in older neighborhoods near downtown. Documenting flood history and repair quality is central to resale and refinance.

Shreveport combines very low acquisition prices with steady rental demand from Barksdale Air Force Base, the medical district and the casino industry. Ranch neighborhoods suit BRRRR and rentals, while South Highlands, Pierremont and Broadmoor support flips. The cheapest houses in high-vacancy areas need careful underwriting because renovation costs can exceed what rents and resale values support.

Across the state, insurance cost can make or break a hold. Roof age and construction, electrical systems, flood zone and elevation all affect premiums and lender DSCR calculations. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review puts those items next to the repair estimate so you can judge the full cost of ownership before buying.

sections.h2: Permits and contractor licensing in Louisiana
sections.body:
Louisiana adopted a statewide uniform construction code after the 2005 hurricanes, but permits and inspections are administered locally by cities and parishes. In New Orleans, the Department of Safety and Permits issues building permits, and the Historic District Landmarks Commission and Vieux Carré Commission review exterior changes in their districts. Baton Rouge and East Baton Rouge Parish operate as a consolidated City-Parish government with a single permitting office. Shreveport runs its own permit office, with zoning and historic preservation handled through the Shreveport-Caddo Metropolitan Planning Commission. Surrounding parishes and smaller cities have their own processes.

Floodplain management is a major part of permitting across the state. Renovations to houses in special flood hazard areas that reach the substantial improvement threshold must bring the structure into compliance with current flood rules, and several parishes strengthened their standards after recent floods.

Contractors are licensed and registered through the Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors. Residential construction above certain contract values requires a residential license, and home improvement work above a lower threshold requires registration. Genstone coordinates trades who hold the credentials each scope needs, pulls permits with the right jurisdiction, prepares historic review submissions where required, schedules inspections and collects lien waivers with every draw.

South Louisiana's hurricane season runs from early summer through fall, and storms such as Katrina, Gustav, Laura, Delta and Ida have shaped the state's housing and insurance market. Renovations in the southern half of the state should get roofs, windows and doors closed in early when work runs into storm season, with materials secured when a storm approaches. After a major storm, demand for roofers and other trades can delay projects across a wide area.

Heavy rainfall is a statewide risk. The 2016 flood in the Baton Rouge region showed that intense rain can flood houses far outside mapped flood zones, and New Orleans streets regularly flood during summer downpours. Drainage, gutters and moisture control belong in most scopes.

Heat and humidity keep mold and termites active for much of the year, and Formosan termites swarm in late spring in the southern parishes. Closed houses deteriorate quickly without air conditioning, and interior finishes need climate control to cure properly.

North Louisiana sees more ice storms, hard freezes, hail and tornadoes than the coast. The February 2021 freeze damaged plumbing across the state, and vacant houses suffered most. Winterizing vacant properties and insulating exposed pipes under raised houses are practical steps everywhere in Louisiana, and expansive clay soils in the north make drainage especially important to foundation repairs.

faqs.q: How does insurance affect renovation decisions in Louisiana?
faqs.a: Insurance has become a major cost for Louisiana property owners, and it affects resale, refinances and cash flow. Insurers commonly focus on roof age and construction, electrical systems, plumbing, flood zone and elevation. Renovations that replace older roofs, remove outdated wiring and document structural repairs can help. Coverage decisions belong to the carrier, so get quotes early, and we will price the items your agent identifies.

faqs.q: What does releveling involve on an older Louisiana house?
faqs.a: Releveling, also called house leveling or shoring, raises the low points of a pier-and-beam house and resets or rebuilds the piers beneath it. It is common in New Orleans because soft soils allow houses to settle unevenly over time. The work should happen before plaster repair, trim, tile and cabinets, and any termite damage or rot found in sills and joists during leveling should be repaired at the same time.

faqs.q: Can I invest in Louisiana from out of state?
faqs.a: Yes. Many of our Louisiana clients live elsewhere. A designated field manager coordinates local trades, handles permits and historic review where needed, and sends photos and milestone updates throughout the project. Draws are released only for completed work, nothing is paid upfront and the final payment follows your approval of the finished property, so you stay in control of decisions without traveling for every stage.
